meta.title: Who really said "Everything that can be invented has been invented"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Charles Duell. The exact line is documented as a joke in Punch's Almanack for 1899, and Duell predicted the opposite in December 1901.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Everything that can be invented has been invented'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Charles Duell. The line is documented as a Punch joke from 1899; the patent commissioner said the opposite. Sources and the debunking trail.

answer.label: Not Charles Duell — a joke from Punch, not a patent commissioner
answer.authorName: Anonymous humorist in Punch’s Almanack for 1899
answer.authorDates: Punch, or the London Charivari · London humour magazine
answer.sourceLine: Charles H. Duell never said this. Quote Investigator finds the whole “patent office is closing, everything is invented” anecdote apocryphal, and the exact sentence is documented as a gag line spoken by a boy in a comic dialogue, “The Coming Century,” in Punch’s Almanack for 1899. Duell, Commissioner of Patents 1898–1901, went on record saying the opposite.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually appears

docMeta.dd: Punch, or the London Charivari, section: December
Comic dialogue — a Genius and a Boy at a future patent office

source.excerpt:
Genius. “Isn’t there a clerk who can examine patents.”
Boy. “Quite unnecessary, Sir. Everything that can be invented has been invented.”
Genius. “Well, I want to leave a novel, a picture, and an idea.”
Boy. “You must be rather old-fashioned, Sir. All sorts of work is done, nowadays, by mental photography.”
trail: December 1883 — Quote Investigator ↗ gives its earliest strong match in The Electrician, vol. 2, no. 12, p. 374: a principal examiner who decided “the inventive power of the human mind had reached its limit.” No commissioner, no Duell.
1899 — the exact modern wording appears as a punchline in Punch’s Almanack for 1899; Wikiquote ↗ lists that almanack as the source and flags the Duell attribution as a misattribution.

December 28, 1901 — Duell, quoted in the Dayton Daily News Saturday Magazine Supplement, predicts that earlier advances “will appear totally insignificant” next to the coming century’s, per Quote Investigator ↗.

July 1940 and 1989 — Eber Jeffery in the Journal of the Patent Office Society found no Patent Office official ever resigned believing nothing was left to invent, a finding recounted in Samuel Sass’s “A Patently False Patent Myth” ↗.
source.excerptNote: Transcription as given by Quote Investigator ↗ from Punch’s Almanack for 1899. It is a joke about the future, not a report of anything a commissioner said.

author.name: Charles Holland Duell
author.kicker: The man who is quoted for the opposite of what he believed
author.heading: Charles Duell, wrongly cast as the patent office pessimist
author.metaLine: 1850–1920 · U.S. Commissioner of Patents, 1898–1901 · later a federal appeals judge
author.bio: Charles Holland Duell (April 13, 1850 – January 29, 1920) was a New York patent lawyer who served as U.S. Commissioner of Patents from 1898 to 1901 and later sat as an Associate Justice of the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. His name became shorthand for short-sightedness because of a sentence he is not documented as ever having spoken. What he actually said, in a December 1901 newspaper feature, was that the advances of the past would “appear totally insignificant” beside what the new century would bring — an almost exact inversion of the line pinned on him.

cite.sourceCitation: “The Coming Century.” Punch’s Almanack for 1899 (Punch, or the London Charivari), section: December. Quoted and dated in Garson O’Toole (Quote Investigator), “Anecdote Origin: Everything That Can Be Invented Has Been Invented,” June 23, 2023. No documented source attributes the sentence to Charles H. Duell.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the blame, and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most durable fake quotes in business writing — a stock illustration of institutional myopia. It has been hung on at least two named commissioners and several anonymous clerks, and none of the versions survives contact with the record.

items.who: Charles H. Duell, U.S. Commissioner of Patents, 1898–1901
items.why: Quote Investigator finds no support for the attribution and notes Duell’s own view was the reverse: in the Dayton Daily News Saturday Magazine Supplement of December 28, 1901, he said “all previous advances…will appear totally insignificant when compared with those which the present century will witness” (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.who: Henry L. Ellsworth, first Commissioner of Patents
items.why: A single rhetorical sentence from his annual report — that the advance of the arts “seems to presage the arrival of that period when human improvement must end” — is read as a literal forecast. Samuel Sass argues it was emphasis on rapid growth, and that Ellsworth’s 1845 resignation cited “pressure of private affairs” (Skeptical Inquirer, 1989 ↗).

items.who: An unnamed patent clerk or examiner who “resigned”
items.why: Told about a principal examiner in The Electrician (December 1883) and about a “chief clerk” in 1848 in a 1938 Esquire piece by Frank Lane Brunton; Eber Jeffery’s July 1940 investigation for the Journal of the Patent Office Society found no such resignation ever occurred (Quote Investigator ↗).

Patently-O reports Sass traced the printed attribution to the 1981 book The Book of Facts and Fallacies, and the Conversable Economist points to 1985 TRW advertisements that put the sentence in Duell’s mouth and dated it 1899 (Conversable Economist ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The exact sentence is documented not in a government report but in a comic dialogue, “The Coming Century,” in Punch’s Almanack for 1899, where a boy uses it to brush off a visiting genius (Wikiquote ↗).

context.heading: Why this fake quote refuses to die
lead: It is the perfect anecdote: a government official so blinkered that he wanted to shut the patent office because human ingenuity had run out. It has been told about at least two real men — Henry L. Ellsworth, the first Commissioner of Patents, and Charles H. Duell — and about an assortment of unnamed clerks and examiners, with the date floating anywhere from the 1830s to 1899. Quote Investigator ↗ traces version after version and finds no substantive documentation behind any of them.

The irony is that the Patent Office was, at exactly this moment, arguing the reverse. Samuel Sass noted that Duell’s own annual report pointed to patent grants rising from 435 in 1837 to 25,527 in 1899 and asked Congress for more resources, as documented in “A Patently False Patent Myth” ↗.
detailsBody: The story was already circulating without Duell’s name attached. Quote Investigator’s earliest strong match is an item in The Electrician (December 1883, vol. 2, no. 12, p. 374) about a principal examiner who around 1843 “came to the mature decision that the work of the patent department must soon come to an end, because the inventive power of the human mind had reached its limit.”

A 1938 Esquire article by Frank Lane Brunton retold it with a “chief clerk” and set it in 1848. Dr. Eber Jeffery investigated the claim in the July 1940 Journal of the Patent Office Society and found no Patent Office official had ever resigned for such a reason, per Sass’s account of Jeffery’s work.

The Duell version in particular got a large modern push from advertising: the Conversable Economist notes 1985 TRW Corporation ads that quoted Duell saying the line “in 1899,” and Patently-O reports that Sass traced the printed attribution back to the 1981 book The Book of Facts and Fallacies by Chris Morgan and David Langford.
context.pull: The man quoted as saying invention was finished spent his term telling Congress it was just getting started.
